title: The History of Fire
summary: Josh and Chuck (with producer Jerry/Dave referenced) explore the prehistory of fire: how and when early hominins first interacted with, gathered, carried, and eventually made fire. They cover animal behavior around fire, the Wonderwork Cave, Koobi Fora-era and other disputed early sites, Gesher Benot Ya'aqov fish cooking, Qesem/Kassim-style hearths, the debate over Neanderthal fire-making, friction and fire-piston methods, birch bark pitch, smoking versus cooking meat, and fire's effects on diet, tools, metallurgy, the AHR gene, circadian rhythms, and disease. The episode ends with a listener mail correction about the Wizard of Oz ruby slippers and the gold standard.
topics: Stuff You Should Know listener mail

segments.title: Opening banter and framing the fire episode
segments.summary: Hosts introduce the episode as a history of how humans came to use and make fire, noting there was no single invention moment and that fire arose in stages.

segments.title: Fire's importance and its late arrival on Earth
segments.summary: They discuss humans as obligate fire users, the impact of cooking, metals, and pottery, theories about language and the campfire, and that fire on Earth depended on atmosphere, vegetation, and lightning, with hominins appearing about six million years ago.

segments.title: Animals, wildfires, and early foraging
segments.summary: Early hominins likely interacted with fire as other animals do; raptors carry burning sticks, predators follow wildfires, and foraging after fires may have led to eating cooked food.

segments.title: Carrying fire and keeping predators away
segments.summary: Humans likely learned to transport fire, using hollows or branches and dung to keep it burning, and fire helped keep predators such as sabertooth tigers away.

segments.title: Stages of fire discovery and when humans began making fire
segments.summary: The hosts outline the stages from foraging to gathering to making fire, noting evidence of fire use over a million years ago but unclear whether humans made it; the key question is when humans started making fire.

segments.title: Break
segments.summary: Short ad break before returning to the episode.

segments.title: Foraging-stage evidence and the Wonderwork Cave
segments.summary: Discussion of Australopithecines possibly using fire around four million years ago, the difficulty of dating the foraging stage, and the Wonderwork Cave in South Africa with burnt bones about a million years old, showing controlled fire use.

segments.title: Early hearths and Gesher Benot Ya'aqov fish cooking
segments.summary: The Kassim Cave in Israel has a hearth dated to about 300,000 years ago. Gesher Benot Ya'aqov in Israel suggests Homo erectus made fire about 780,000 years ago and cooked fish, determined by tooth analysis showing a controlled roast.

segments.title: Rising Star Cave, Zhoukoudian, and disputed sites
segments.summary: Rising Star Cave in South Africa possibly shows fire use by Homo naledi around 335,000 years ago, though disputed. Zhoukoudian Cave's 1920s hearth claims were later reexamined and revisited in the 2010s.

segments.title: Did Neanderthals make fire?
segments.summary: Debate over Neanderthals: French sites show more fire traces in warmer periods; ash buildup suggests they kept fires going rather than rekindling; but birch bark pitch and manganese dioxide suggest they may have known how to start fires.

segments.title: Fire-making methods: percussion, friction, fire piston
segments.summary: Percussion sparks from flint, the fire drill and friction methods, and the fire piston, which heats air by rapid compression to ignite tinder. Hosts reflect on how birch pitch was first discovered.

segments.title: Break
segments.summary: Short ad break before returning to the episode.

segments.title: Fire and migration, light, and birch bark pitch tools
segments.summary: Fire enabled humans to move into colder northern latitudes and gave light for exploring caves and the darkness. Discussion of birch bark pitch as an adhesive for arrows and the Make It Primitive channel, plus the show Alone.
topics: fire and migration to cold climates

segments.title: Smoking versus cooking meat and hearth types
segments.summary: Hosts speculate that smoking meat from large megafauna like mammoths may have been an early use of fire, noting it is conjecture based on animal size and evidence like tool and teeth marks. They consider different hearths for pottery and socializing.

segments.title: Hearths, pottery, and kiln cooking
segments.summary: Permanent or semi-permanent hearths around four hundred thousand years ago; hosts joke about cooking in a kiln and pottery firing.

segments.title: How fire shaped metallurgy, biology, and sleep
segments.summary: Fire enabled smelting copper and the Stone-to-Metal Ages transition. A gene mutation, the AHR gene, may have reduced sensitivity to smoke. Humans' circadian rhythms shifted to being more alert in the evening due to fire.

segments.title: Fire and disease spread
segments.summary: Huddling around fires may have spread disease; a study links tuberculosis emergence to around the time humans controlled fire.

segments.title: Closing banter
segments.summary: Hosts wrap up the fire history with light banter.

segments.title: Listener mail: gold standard correction
segments.summary: Liz from Cleveland writes that the ruby slippers in the Wizard of Oz book were silver, representing the silver standard, and the movie changed them to ruby for Technicolor. Hosts thank her.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts invite listeners to send email to Stuff Podcasts at iHeartRadio dot com and close the episode.
